content:
Hello everyone,

I am an undergraduate student interested in the formalisation of math. I have attended Lean classes this year, and now I'm working with Lean as a part of a REU.

Recently I have been looking at graph theory and how it is done, and thought that it might be a good first experience with trying to contribute myself. I have written up some very basic things which I found to be missing here:

  • deleting a dart from a loop walk to get a "subwalk" going between the dart's two endpoints; this seems like a very natural operation to me, but I had trouble targeting a specific dart of a walk in the current API (although I guess it could be done with idxOf), so the most elegant solution seemed to be just defining it from the ground up;
  • the Hasse graph of a linear order is acyclic (in particular path graphs);
  • deleting a leaf preserves acyclicity and trees;
  • disjoint union of graphs preserves acyclicity

and some other lemmas.

So, my question is, what do I do now? Should I simply fork mathlib and make a new PR? I am not really that confident, this is my first attempt at writing library-like code (and I am still quite new to Lean). I will be glad for any feedback on my efforts (in fact, I was hoping to get some by this post)!

Secondly, I would like to try doing a bigger project in graph theory. I know that there is still a lot missing, but at the same time, there is a lot of active effort on many different topics. How do I get started in this regard? Are there any known interesting theorems/theories that no one is working on, or should I reach out to someone for collaboration?

Your first bullet point I essentially have in proof-bench (secret repo, sorry!). Your last two bullet points are in open PRs. I don't know of anyone work on the second bullet point, so yeah please try showing it and open a PR when you're done!

Thanks for letting me know! It seems that I had looked only at the ready-for-review pull requests.

However, regarding deleting leaves from leaves, I believe only the fact that this preserves connectedness and acyclicity is in mathlib? I also proved that adding leaves preserves this (which is admittedly the less interesting direction) to have an equivalence.

I went ahead and opened a PR for the Hasse graphs of linear orders. Other than they are acyclic, I added a "discrete intermediate value theorem": when one has a walk between two vertices of such a graph, it visits all the vertices between them.
